node.title: Inner mitochondrial membrane role
node.canonical_question: Why is the inner mitochondrial membrane important for ATP production?
node.summary: The inner membrane is impermeable to protons. This forces protons through ATP synthase, coupling the gradient to ATP production.

seeds.question: How does the proton gradient build up across the inner membrane?
What would happen to ATP production if the inner membrane became leaky?
How does the structure of the inner membrane differ from the outer membrane?

parsed.rendering_md:
The inner mitochondrial membrane is critically tight — it is essentially impermeable to protons (H+ ions). This impermeability is the physical foundation for ATP synthesis.

The electron transport chain (Complexes I, III, and IV) actively pumps protons from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space. Because the inner membrane will not let protons leak back passively, they accumulate there, building up both a concentration gradient and an electrical gradient (the membrane potential). Together these form the proton-motive force.

The only efficient route for protons to flow back down this gradient is through ATP synthase, a protein embedded in the inner membrane. As protons flow through ATP synthase's F0 channel, the resulting rotation drives the F1 catalytic head to bind ADP and inorganic phosphate and release ATP.

If the membrane were leaky — if protons could slip through freely — the gradient would collapse. There would be no driving force to spin ATP synthase, and oxidative phosphorylation would stop even if the electron transport chain kept running. This is exactly what chemical uncouplers such as 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) do: they carry protons across the membrane outside of ATP synthase, dissipating the gradient as heat instead of ATP.

In short, the tightness of the inner membrane is what couples electron transport to ATP synthesis. Without it, the two processes become uncoupled and energy is wasted.
